content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler multiple vegetables, Stage 2 is a ready‑to‑eat baby puree made from a blend of vegetables, designed for infants aged 6–12 months (stage 2 of weaning). The puree contains carrot, broccoli, cauliflower and pumpkin, steamed and blended to a smooth consistency without added salt, sugar or preservatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Combining several vegetables provides a broader spectrum of vitamins and minerals than single‑vegetable purees.
The vegetables undergo double steam cooking, preserving most of their nutrients.
The puree is free from gluten and dairy, making it safe for children with common food allergies.
Packaging is made from BPA‑free plastic and can be reused.
Each 80 g serving meets the daily requirement for vitamin A and vitamin C for infants.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A from carrot and pumpkin supports vision development and the infant's immune system.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Broccoli and cauliflower are high in vitamin C, which aids immune function and iron absorption.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables helps establish a healthy gut microbiome and eases digestion.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: No added salt makes the product safe for the delicate kidneys of young babies.

items.title: Easy to swallow
items.content: The smooth texture reduces choking risk and encourages independent feeding.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Although the product contains no common allergens, some infants may react to certain vegetables. Discontinue use if rash, swelling, or other symptoms appear.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the puree refrigerated and consume within 48 hours.

items.title: Not suitable for children over 12 months without medical advice
items.content: The intensity of some vegetable flavors may be too strong for older toddlers without gradual introduction.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The puree is ready to eat straight from the pouch. If desired, gently warm in the microwave (no more than 30 seconds), stir well, and let cool to a warm temperature. It can be thinned with breast milk or formula for a looser consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened pouches in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 48 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Italian, Grecian and Armenian breads are traditional bakery products, each with distinct recipes, baking methods and flavor profiles. Italian bread is often made from wheat flour with olive oil and dry yeast, giving a crisp crust and soft crumb. Grecian bread such as pita has a thin crust and a hollow interior that can be used as a pocket for fillings. Armenian lavash is thin, flexible and usually baked on an open fire, which imparts a characteristic smoky aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Italian ciabatta gets its name from the word “ciabatta”, meaning “slipper”, because of its shape.
Traditional Greek pita is baked in a “sac” oven that reaches 300 °C, creating the signature pocket.
Armenian lavash is often baked in a tandoor‑like clay oven where the dough sticks to the hot walls and quickly inflates.
In all three cultures bread is a symbol of hospitality and is usually served at the beginning of a meal.
Italy boasts over 200 regional bread varieties, each with its own ingredients and fermentation technique.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides slowly digestible energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber (especially whole‑grain versions)
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and nurtures a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2 and niacin are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals: iron, magnesium, phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are essential for blood formation, muscle function and bone health.

items.title: Low sodium content (when not added)
items.content: Homemade, unsalted bread is suitable for low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White bread raises blood sugar quickly, which is undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Commercial breads often contain a lot of salt; excess intake may increase blood pressure.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some industrial breads are enriched with flavor enhancers and preservatives that can cause allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bread can be enjoyed on its own, used for sandwiches, served alongside soups and salads, or turned into croutons, breadcrumbs and breaded coatings. Thin Armenian lavash works well for wraps, while Italian ciabatta is often paired with olive oil and balsamic vinegar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bread in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag; thaw at room temperature or briefly warm in the oven before serving.

chicken-breast-baked-broiled-or-roasted-.title: Chicken breast, baked, broiled, or roasted with marinade, skin eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean cut of poultry meat, high in protein and low in calories. When cooked with a flavorful marinade and the skin left on, it stays juicy and gains additional taste from herbs and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides almost twice the protein of most red‑meat cuts.
Marinating helps retain moisture and enhances flavor, especially for baking or grilling.
The skin is rich in collagen, which can be beneficial for skin and joint health when cooked properly.
Traditional oven roasting is done at 180‑200 °C for about 20‑25 minutes, depending on thickness.
When grilling, removing the skin beforehand reduces fat content if a low‑fat diet is desired.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: A 100‑g serving delivers roughly 31 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Skin‑less chicken breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B3 (niacin) and B6 aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Chicken provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of high protein and moderate calories helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Raw chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C to ensure safety.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to chicken proteins and should avoid consumption.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Commercial marinades can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium or homemade versions if sodium intake is a concern.

items.title: Potential carcinogen formation
items.content: High‑heat grilling can create heterocyclic amines; cook at moderate temperatures and avoid charring.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Marinate the breast in olive oil, lemon juice, garlic and herbs, then bake, broil, or grill until the internal temperature reaches 74 °C. The skin can be left on for extra flavor or removed before serving. Serve with vegetables, whole grains, or slice for salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw chicken breast refrigerated at +1‑4 °C for up to 2 days, or freeze at ‑18 °C for up to 9 months. Cooked breast should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach dip is a creamy sauce made from fresh spinach, cream cheese, yogurt, and seasonings. It has a mild, slightly tangy flavor with a distinctive spinach aroma and works well as a snack dip or accompaniment to main dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach dip is commonly served with crackers, vegetable sticks, or as a sauce for fish and chicken dishes.
Traditional recipes often include feta or cottage cheese, giving the dip a smooth texture.
Spinach retains most of its nutrients with minimal heat treatment, so many dips are prepared from raw fresh spinach.
In the United States, spinach dip gained popularity in the 1990s alongside the health‑food movement.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Spinach provides a high amount of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Iron from spinach supports normal hemoglobin levels and energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in spinach help protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low‑calorie option
items.content: A dip based on yogurt and cream cheese is relatively low in calories, making it suitable for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from spinach promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream cheese and yogurt may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergy.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared dip may contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dip chilled with vegetable sticks, crackers, or use it as a sauce for baked meat, fish, and potatoes. It can also be spread on sandwiches or used as a filling for wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep spinach dip in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. Discard if it develops off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked tomatoes are the fruits of the tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum) that have been boiled until tender. Heat treatment retains most of their vitamins and minerals while making them easier to digest. They are used in sauces, soups, stews, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes belong to the nightshade family and are botanically classified as berries with juicy flesh.
Cooking increases the bioavailability of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Cooked tomatoes are a staple in many world cuisines, from Italian marinara to Russian shchi.
They contain about 90 % water, making them a low‑calorie food.
Tomatoes can be grown in greenhouses, allowing year‑round production.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a strong antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Cooked tomatoes retain a good amount of vitamin C, which boosts immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports proper heart function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to tomatoes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tomatoes can aggravate heartburn in individuals with high stomach acidity.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic tomatoes, rinse them thoroughly to reduce any pesticide residue.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked tomatoes can be added to sauces, soups, stews, pizza, casseroles, and salads. They are also used as purees or as the base for tomato paste. Serve them warm or chilled.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tomatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portion‑size bags—they will retain flavor and nutrients.
